newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan's Yulon ready for Korean car challenge.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's Yulon ready for Korean car challenge.

text.p: Yulon Motor Co, which makes Nissan cars in Taiwan, said on Monday it was ready to meet the challenge of car imports from South Korea.
South Korea said on Saturday that Taiwan was lifting a ban on Korean car imports dating to 1992, when Seoul stunned its anti-communist ally by switching diplomatic ties to China.

Seoul's trade ministry said Taiwan agreed to take 7,000 units this year under a quota that calls for a 10 percent increase every year. Under the agreement, the quota will be raised to 10,000 in the first year after Taiwan joins the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and by 20 percent a year thereafter.

"We have anticipated more foreign car imports because of Taiwan's intention to join the WTO, but the imports of South Korean cars are earlier than expected," Yulon vice-president Chen Kuo-rong told a news conference.
"It will surely be a tough challenge...The outward changes are impossible to control, so we can only re-engineer our inward part," Chen said.

"Yulon has for years prepared for WTO challenge, and has strived to improve quality, cost and service. If you can do well in these things, you survive. If you make some mistakes, (you will be) miserable."
Taiwan also plans to open its car market to imports from Japan, Malaysia, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Australia and South Africa, even before its entry to the WTO.
Taiwan wants to join the WTO in 1997 but faces U.S. and other Western opposition over trade barriers as well as rival China's determination not to allow the island's entry before its own.

Liu said Yulon had been doing extremely well since introducing its new Cefiro model, with net profits in the first nine months of T$1.01 billion (US$36.6 million) compared with just T$89 million (US$3.2 million in the same period last year.
Yulon introduced a 2,000-cc Cefiro in February and a 3,000-cc version on October 5. It expects to sell 25,000 of the cars this year.
Sales in January-September rose to T$27.55 billion, up 12.5 percent from T$24.5 billion in the same period last year, despite Taiwan's car market as a whole having slipped 16.9 percent, Liu said.
The company said sales of locally made cars had fallen 12.5 percent in the same period and sales of imported cars by 30.4 percent.
It forecast Taiwan car sales would fall 13 percent to 467,000 units this year.
But Wu Hsin-fa, head of Yulon's business department, forecast that 1997 car sales would grow three percent to 481,000 cars.
Yulon will introduce a 1,600-cc Nissan Sentra on November 16, four days before its global debut in Australia, Wu added.
